Affected Functions
Version
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::crt_coefficient
  • <0.10.4
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::from_components
  • <0.10.4
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::from_p_q
  • <0.10.4
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::from_primes
  • <0.10.4
sad_rsa::RsaPrivateKey::validate
  • <0.10.4

Description

RsaPrivateKey private-key construction, validation, and serialization can panic across three classes of inputs, as well as when re-encoding certain valid keys:

  • RsaPrivateKey::from_components and PKCS#1 or PKCS#8 private-key decoding (DER or PEM) can panic during validation when a supplied factor equals 1, because RsaPrivateKey::validate() let a factor of 1 reach a later check that panicked.
  • RsaPrivateKey::from_primes and RsaPrivateKey::from_p_q can panic during construction when a supplied factor is 0, 1, or even.
  • Prime recovery in RsaPrivateKey::from_components can panic when the private exponent is 0.
  • For a key, including a valid one, whose first prime occupies more limbs than the second, crt_coefficient, to_pkcs1_der, to_pkcs8_der, and serde serialization can panic.

An application that imports untrusted private keys or factors, or re-encodes such keys, can lose a worker, or the whole process when built with panic = "abort". Public-key parsing is not affected.

Fixed in 0.10.4, which rejects factors below 2, even factors, repeated factors, and a zero private exponent during prime recovery, and computes the CRT coefficient and re-encodes valid two-prime keys when the first prime occupies more limbs than the second.

If you cannot upgrade to 0.10.4, isolate the entire import, construction, CRT calculation, or serialization in a separate process and treat an abnormal exit as an operation failure, or use catch_unwind around the entire operation when panics unwind.

Affected Functions
Version
tokio_rate_limit::tonic_middleware::IpKeyExtractor::extract
  • >=0.5.0, <0.11.1

Description

tonic_middleware::IpKeyExtractor is documented as rate limiting gRPC requests by client IP address, but on a standard tonic server it keys on client-supplied x-forwarded-for and x-real-ip headers. In 0.5.0–0.9.1, the extractor reads those headers directly; in 0.10.0–0.11.0, it first checks for a bare std::net::SocketAddr request extension—which tonic::transport::Server never supplies, as it provides TcpConnectInfo instead—and falls back to the same headers. Direct clients can therefore choose their rate-limit key to bypass per-IP rate limits and increase the number of tracked keys; without forwarding headers, 0.5.0–0.9.1 allow requests without limiting them and 0.10.0–0.11.0 reject them by default unless .fail_open() is enabled.

Applications are affected if they use GrpcRateLimitLayer with IpKeyExtractor (the tonic-support feature). The HTTP middleware's IpKeyExtractor reads ConnectInfo<SocketAddr> and is not affected.

Version 0.11.1 fixes IpKeyExtractor to honor a server-supplied SocketAddr override first and then read the TCP peer address from tonic's TcpConnectInfo (which tonic::transport::Server attaches to plaintext connections and connections using its built-in TLS), without ever reading forwarding headers. Deployments behind a trusted proxy can use the new opt-in ForwardedIpKeyExtractor, which reads a single configured header (x-forwarded-for or x-real-ip) and is only correct when that proxy sets the header as documented.

If you cannot upgrade to 0.11.1, use a custom key extractor that reads the peer IP from tonic's connection information for the transport in use (including TLS) and rejects requests without a verified peer address before invoking the limiter, or restrict backend access to a trusted proxy that strips all incoming x-forwarded-for and x-real-ip fields and sets one x-forwarded-for value to the verified client IP on every request.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0585: Vulnerability in pqcrypto-mlkem
entry.summary: ML-KEM does not perform the FIPS 203 input checks
entry.content:

RUSTSEC-2026-0585

ML-KEM does not perform the FIPS 203 input checks
Reported
November 20, 2026
Issued
November 20, 2026
Package
pqcrypto-mlkem (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • crypto-failure
Keywords
#ml-kem #fips203 #input-validation
References
  • https://github.com/RatioLabsEU/pqc-field-notes/tree/main/advisories/2026-mlkem-input-validation
Patched
no patched versions
Affected Functions
Version
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem1024::decapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem1024::encapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem512::decapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem512::encapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem768::decapsulate
  • <=0.1.1
pqcrypto_mlkem::mlkem768::encapsulate
  • <=0.1.1

Description

pqcrypto-mlkem wraps PQClean's ML-KEM implementation, which does not perform the input checks required by FIPS 203:

  • encapsulation does not perform the encapsulation key modulus check (section 7.2), so encapsulation keys with coefficients that are not reduced modulo q are accepted;
  • decapsulation does not perform the decapsulation key hash check (section 7.3), so a decapsulation key whose stored hash or embedded encapsulation key has been altered is accepted.

With the Wycheproof ML-KEM vectors, 108 / 112 / 116 invalid encapsulation keys (ML-KEM-512 / -768 / -1024) and 2 invalid decapsulation keys per parameter set are accepted.

This does not disclose key material. It is a FIPS 203 non-conformance, and an affected implementation can disagree with a conforming one about which keys are valid.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2026-0161) and no patched version is expected. Migrating to a maintained implementation, such as the ml-kem crate, is recommended.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0586: Vulnerability in pqcrypto-mldsa
entry.summary: ML-DSA verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the `avx2` feature
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0586

ML-DSA verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the avx2 feature
Reported
November 20, 2026
Issued
November 20, 2026
Package
pqcrypto-mldsa (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • crypto-failure
Keywords
#ml-dsa #signature #verification #avx2
References
  • https://github.com/RatioLabsEU/pqc-field-notes/tree/main/advisories/2026-mldsa-avx2-verifier
  • https://github.com/pq-crystals/dilithium/issues/113
Patched
no patched versions
Affected Architectures
  • x86_64
Affected Functions
Version
pqcrypto_mldsa::mldsa44::verify_detached_signature
  • <=0.1.2
pqcrypto_mldsa::mldsa65::verify_detached_signature
  • <=0.1.2
pqcrypto_mldsa::mldsa87::verify_detached_signature
  • <=0.1.2

Description

With the default avx2 feature on x86_64 (non-Windows) and a CPU that supports AVX2, pqcrypto-mldsa verifies signatures with PQClean's AVX2 implementation of ML-DSA. That implementation predates two upstream fixes (pq-crystals/dilithium#113, 3 June 2026):

  • the verifier does not check that the infinity norm of z is below γ1 − β (FIPS 204, Algorithm 8, line 13), so it accepts signatures that conforming verifiers reject;
  • use_hint_avx() mishandles a boundary case, so one class of valid signatures is rejected.

Creating an accepted out-of-bound signature requires the private key. The practical effect is that verification results differ between this crate with AVX2 and conforming implementations, including this crate without AVX2.

The Wycheproof ML-DSA verification vectors reproduce both defects: with AVX2, 37 / 41 / 49 invalid vectors (ML-DSA-44 / -65 / -87) are accepted and one valid vector per parameter set is rejected.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2026-0166) and no patched version is expected. Disabling the avx2 feature avoids the affected code. Migrating to a maintained implementation, such as the ml-dsa crate, is recommended.

Description

Before writing an entry whose path goes through a symlink, ZipArchive::extract checks the symlink's target against the destination directory. That check compares the paths as text and does not follow symlinks, and from 7.2.0 it drops the root and prefix of an absolute target before comparing. Symlinks taken from the archive were created without any check of their targets.

A crafted archive can first create a symlink that points outside the destination, then a second symlink whose target looks like a path inside the destination but goes through the first one, and then a file entry under the second symlink. The file is written outside the destination directory, for example over an existing file in the user's home directory, and extract still returns Ok(()). On Windows, a target on another drive or share whose path otherwise matches the destination passes the check directly (creating symlinks there needs Developer Mode or administrator rights). The attacker has to know or guess the absolute path of the destination directory.

This affects ZipArchive::extract and ZipArchive::extract_unwrapped_root_dir.

The fix resolves symlink targets one component at a time from the canonicalized destination, following symlinks on the way, and refuses to create a symlink, or write through one, that leads outside the destination.

entry.summary: `ZipStreamReader` extracts entries under local-header names that can differ from the central directory

RUSTSEC-2026-0548

ZipStreamReader extracts entries under local-header names that can differ from the central directory
Reported

Package
zip (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • privilege-escalation
Keywords
#parser-differential #local-file-header #central-directory
Aliases
  • CVE-2026-115905
  • GHSA-m665-v7pm-7grj
References
  • https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/commit/8068ab480ccf8daa7411424e365fcdbe6d09443e
Patched
  • >=9.0.5

Description

A ZIP archive names each entry twice: in the local file header in front of the entry's data, and in the central directory at the end of the archive. ZipArchive lists and opens entries by their central-directory names. ZipStreamReader::visit and ZipStreamReader::extract, like read_zipfile_from_stream, read the local headers in order and use the local-header names without comparing them with the central directory.

An archive can therefore show one set of file names to code that inspects it with ZipArchive and write files under other names when it is extracted with ZipStreamReader. If an application checks an archive one way and extracts it the other way, an attacker can get files written or overwritten inside the destination directory that the check never saw.

The fix adds an opt-in check. ZipStreamReader::enforce_header_consistency(true) compares each local header with its central-directory entry (name, sizes, CRC-32, compression method, flags and modification time) and fails extraction on a mismatch; ZipReadOptions::enforce_header_consistency(true) and ZipArchive::validate_header_consistency() do the same for ZipArchive. The check is off by default, so upgrading alone does not change what ZipStreamReader::new(...) extracts: applications that extract untrusted archives with ZipStreamReader need to turn it on.

Description

A client kept the token from a Retry packet without any length limit and put it into the header of every Initial packet it sent afterwards. Initial datagrams are 1200 bytes. When the token and connection IDs left no room for the minimum payload, PacketBuilder::new computed a minimum packet size larger than the maximum, which only a debug assertion checked. On the next poll_transmit, debug builds panic, and release builds try to allocate more than 10 GiB in one call. With longer tokens the allocation fails and the process aborts.

A matching Retry packet can be built from the client's first Initial alone. The attacker can therefore be the server being contacted, or anyone who sees that Initial and can answer before the server does. Every application that makes outgoing connections with quinn-proto is affected, including all quinn clients. Servers do not process Retry packets.

The fix closes the connection with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION when an Initial token leaves too little room for frames. That covers Retry tokens and cached address-validation tokens, since both come from the peer. It also reserves room for CONNECTION_CLOSE after large Initial headers. Both changes are in 0.11.19.

Depending on the runtime, the endpoint runs out of memory, stops accepting new connections, or keeps busy indefinitely, even after the peer has gone away. Clients and servers that accept peer-initiated bidirectional streams are affected. Unidirectional streams are not.

Patched
  • >=4.2.5
  • >=4.1.9, <4.2.0
  • >=3.3.5, <4.0.0

Description

The MathML text integration points (mi, mo, mn, ms, mtext) and SVG foreignObject can be made to contain a tag in the other one's namespace (a MathML integration point with a child in the SVG namespace, or vice versa) without the root tag that switches out of the HTML namespace. If the attacker can construct input that parses differently in as HTML than as foreign XML, they can inject arbitrary JavaScript code into the user's browser.

For example:

  • The user writes <math><mi><svg><gadget></svg></mi></math>.
  • The application enables math, mi, and the gadget, but not svg.
  • Ammonia filters the input to <math><mi><gadget></mi></math>.
  • Because svg is now gone, the gadget switches from being parsed as SVG to being parsed as HTML.
  • The gadget is written in such a way that it exploits the parsing differences between HTML and MathML.

As far as we know, the gadget can only be written using a tag that is parsed as raw text in HTML. These elements are:

  • title
  • textarea
  • xmp
  • iframe
  • noembed
  • noframes
  • plaintext
  • noscript
  • style
  • script

Applications that do not explicitly allow any of these tags should not be affected, since none are allowed by default.

This vulnerability was reported by Roger Meyer.

Description

Some targets read one datagram per recvmsg call instead of using recvmmsg: Apple platforms without the fast-apple-datapath feature, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Solaris and illumos, and from 0.6 also DragonFly BSD, Redox and GNU/Hurd. On these targets the receive loop set up its msghdr only once and looked at the MSG_TRUNC flag before checking whether recvmsg had failed. After a datagram larger than the receive buffer was dropped, a following EAGAIN still saw the old truncation flag. The loop then kept issuing non-blocking receives instead of returning WouldBlock.

When the receive buffer is smaller than a datagram that arrives, a remote sender can keep the task that drives the socket busy, before any QUIC packet authentication. The loop ends only when a later datagram fits in the buffer. Whether an application is exposed therefore depends on the receive buffer size it uses. Linux, Android, FreeBSD and Windows use other receive paths and are not affected.

The fix rebuilds the header before every recvmsg call and returns receive errors before checking the truncation flag. It is in 0.5.16 and 0.6.3.
